chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: A chat widget that runs entirely in your browser
chunks.text: Pilot of the client-side OpenRouter widget — no backend, built to drop into any static GitHub Pages site. This documentation site is a live demo of a framework-free chat widget you can add to a static website with a single script tag. There is no server behind the chat: everything — signing in to OpenRouter, holding the key, calling the model, rendering the answer — happens in your browser.

chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text: Tap Ask in the corner, then Connect OpenRouter . The widget runs an OAuth PKCE flow and brings back a scoped sk-or key. Your messages go straight to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions with streaming. The default model is openrouter/free (“Auto (free models only)”), so a default chat costs nothing; you can switch to openrouter/auto (“Auto (best available)”, may bill paid models) from the picker.

chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: It reads this page, and the whole site
chunks.text: The widget sends the visible text of the page you are on as context, so it can answer questions about what you are reading. It also loads a small site-index.json built at deploy time and does lightweight in-browser retrieval (BM25) across every page, so it can answer site-wide questions and cite the page it used. Try asking: "Where is my OpenRouter key stored?" , "Why is a client-side key an XSS risk?" , or "Who pays for the model calls?" — the answer should link to the matching page.

chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: Try a tool call: the chat can change this color
chunks.text: The chat can do more than answer questions. It can also change the color below. The swatch starts at #1f6feb. Connect OpenRouter, then ask for a change, for example "Make it teal" or "Set the color to #ff8800" . A sample you may see in a tool form is #3366ff. That sample is not the starting color. Pick a color Reset color Color: #1f6feb Recent tool calls

chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: How the tool call works
chunks.text: This page defines three tools in JavaScript: set_color , get_color and reset_color . Each tool has a name, a short description, a JSON schema for its input, and a schema for the result. set_color lists the hex form and the allowed color names in that input schema. The color field description is short. The names stay in the schema list. When you send a message, the widget sends the tool list to OpenRouter together with your question. If the model wants to change the color, it replies with a tool call. A tool call is a tool name and its arguments in JSON. The widget runs the tool in your browser, and the color changes. The chat shows the tool name, the arguments and the result.

chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: How the tool call works
chunks.text: The widget sends the result back to OpenRouter. Then the model writes its final answer. The widget stops after four rounds of tool calls. Tool calls work only with the OpenRouter provider. With the other providers, the chat answers with text only. Some free models cannot use tools. If you get an error, send the message again or pick another model.

chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: The same tools for an outside assistant (WebMCP)
chunks.text: WebMCP is a proposed web standard. It lets a page offer its tools to an AI assistant in the browser, for example a browser agent or an extension. This page registers the same three tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . The widget and WebMCP use the same tool code and the same input rules. Each tool also says what it returns. The result schema documents that shape for tests and for future browsers. Chrome 156 does not pass that schema on. The page also registers two read-only guides. One lists the public pages on this site. The other lists the headings and links on this page. Neither guide reads keys, cookies, or saved chat.

chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: The same tools for an outside assistant (WebMCP)
chunks.text: The page tools guide explains the same idea for the rest of the site. Your browser does not support WebMCP, so only the chat widget can use these tools. The rest of the page works as usual. To try WebMCP, use Chrome 146 or later. Open chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , set it to Enabled, and relaunch Chrome. Then open this page with an agent that supports WebMCP, for example the Model Context Tool Inspector extension from Chrome.

chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: The safety rule
chunks.text: The tools can change only the color on this page. They cannot read your key, send data or run code. The color must be a hex value or a name from a fixed list of 31 CSS color names. That list stays in the tool input schema. The field description stays short. An assistant can read the names from the schema before calling the tool. If the input is not valid, the tool returns an error and the allowed names, and changes nothing. The page never runs code that the model writes. The model can only choose a tool from the list and give its arguments. The chat shows each tool call as plain text, not as HTML. A tool result cannot add a script to the page.

chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: Security model
chunks.text: The pilot pages are locked down with a meta-tag CSP : script-src 'self' and connect-src 'self' https://openrouter.ai , with no inline scripts, no inline styles and no eval. Model output is rendered through the vendored marked + DOMPurify pipeline, so a hostile reply cannot inject script. See the linked pages for where the key lives, the XSS trade-off, and who pays. This widget is deliberately separate from the Browser Tutor's own server-side OpenRouter session. It uses its own btw_* sessionStorage keys and never touches the tutor's login cookie or saved chat.

chunks.title: Who pays for the model — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Who pays for the model calls
chunks.text: The visitor pays. The widget uses your OpenRouter account via a key you authorize through OAuth, so every chat request is billed to your OpenRouter credits — never to the site owner. The site owner ships only static files and has no API key of their own in the page.

chunks.title: Who pays for the model — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Default and free models
chunks.text: The default model is openrouter/free (“Auto (free models only)”): it only routes to free models, so a default chat costs nothing, but free models share a rate-limited pool and can be slower or return 429s. If you pick openrouter/auto (“Auto (best available)”) it routes to the best available model and may pick a paid model , billing your credits. The picker also lists individual :free models.

chunks.title: Who pays for the model — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Abuse and cost exposure
chunks.text: Because there is no server, the only cost exposure is the visitor's own key. There is no shared budget to drain and no server-side rate limit to tune; the natural limit is each visitor's own credits and OpenRouter's own per-key limits. To stop spending, tap Disconnect (which drops the key from this tab) and revoke the key at openrouter.ai/settings/keys . A browser assistant can read a short guide to this page. The guide lists headings and the other docs pages. It does not read keys, cookies, or saved chat.

chunks.title: Privacy — what leaves your browser — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Privacy: what leaves your browser
chunks.text: Two things leave your browser, and only when you chat: the text you type, and the context the widget attaches — the visible text of the current page plus a few retrieved excerpts from this site's site-index.json . These go directly to OpenRouter over HTTPS, under your key. Nothing goes to the site owner, because there is no backend.

chunks.title: Privacy — what leaves your browser — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Page text is treated as data
chunks.text: The current page's text and the retrieved site excerpts are wrapped in explicit delimiters and stripped of control characters before being sent, and the system prompt tells the model to treat them as data, not instructions. This reduces prompt-injection from page content.

chunks.title: Privacy — what leaves your browser — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Where things are stored
chunks.text: Your key, chosen model and chat history live in this tab's sessionStorage and are gone when the tab closes. The only localStorage entries are a one-time sign-in verifier (deleted on return, 10-minute cap) and, only if you opt in, a 7-day remembered key. See where your key lives for the exact key names.

chunks.title: Privacy — what leaves your browser — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Chrome on-device option (pilot)
chunks.text: In desktop Chrome with built-in AI, you can pick “Chrome On-device” in the provider picker. The model then runs on your own device: your question and the page text are not sent to any model server, and there is no key or sign-in. The one-time model download is several gigabytes and starts only when you tap the download button. This site's site-index.json is still fetched from this site's own origin, and it is English only. A browser assistant can read a short guide to this page. The guide lists headings and the other docs pages. It does not read keys, cookies, or saved chat.

chunks.title: Where your OpenRouter key lives — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Where your OpenRouter key lives
chunks.text: When you connect OpenRouter in this widget, the issued sk-or key is stored in sessionStorage under the key name btw_or_key . sessionStorage is scoped to this one browser tab and this one origin, and it is cleared automatically when you close the tab .

chunks.title: Where your OpenRouter key lives — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Why sessionStorage and not a cookie
chunks.text: A cookie would be sent to the server on every request — but there is no server here, and we never want the key to leave your browser except in the Authorization header to OpenRouter itself. sessionStorage keeps the key client-side, per-tab, and short-lived. The Disconnect button wipes btw_or_key , the cached user id, the model choice and the chat history immediately.

chunks.title: Where your OpenRouter key lives — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: The sign-in round-trip
chunks.text: When you tap Connect OpenRouter , the widget creates a one-time PKCE code_verifier and a random state and keeps them in localStorage under btw_pkce for at most 10 minutes (OpenRouter's code lifetime). It is localStorage rather than sessionStorage because on phones the return from OpenRouter can open in a new tab , a Custom Tab or an installed-app window, where this tab's sessionStorage does not exist. The entry is deleted the moment the return is handled, the state must match, and the code is scrubbed from the address bar. The verifier alone is useless without the code.

chunks.title: Where your OpenRouter key lives — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Optional: remember on this device
chunks.text: By default the key is session-only. If you tick Remember on this device for 7 days , a copy goes to localStorage ( btw_or_key_persist ) with a 7-day expiry, so it survives closing the tab and is picked up by your other tabs. That is more convenient but riskier: until it expires, any script running on this site could read it. Only use it on your own device; Disconnect wipes it.

chunks.title: Where your OpenRouter key lives — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: What is NOT used
chunks.text: Apart from the short-lived sign-in entry above and the opt-in remember copy, the key never goes to localStorage , and the widget never touches the tutor's own login cookie bt_sess or its saved transcript bt_chat . It only uses its own btw_ -prefixed keys. Conversation history also lives only in sessionStorage and disappears when the tab closes. Rule of thumb: a key in sessionStorage is readable by any JavaScript running on this origin. That is the visitor's own risk, which the XSS page explains. A browser assistant can read a short guide to this page. The guide lists headings and the other docs pages. It does not read keys, cookies, or saved chat.

chunks.title: Page tools for browser assistants — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Page tools for browser assistants
chunks.text: How this site offers tools to an assistant in the browser, and how the tutor limits the tools on the server.

chunks.title: Page tools for browser assistants — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: What WebMCP is
chunks.text: WebMCP is a proposed way for a web page to offer tools to an assistant that runs in the browser. The page calls document.modelContext.registerTool . The assistant can then see the tool and run it. In Chrome today this needs a testing flag. Use Chrome 146 or later. Open chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , set it to Enabled, and relaunch Chrome. The assistant does not have to be one this site built. Gemini in Chrome can call the tools. A browser agent can call them. The Model Context Tool Inspector extension can list them and run them by hand.

chunks.title: Page tools for browser assistants — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: What each page offers
chunks.text: The read-only tools do not read cookies, web storage, or saved chat. The color tools are the only ones that change the page, and they change only the example color. Every page offers get_site_guide . It lists the public pages on this site. It returns the path, the title, and a short summary for each page. The home page summary says that sign-in is needed to see what the browser reveals. The signed-out home page also offers get_landing_guide . It says you need to sign in before this site can show what the browser reveals. It returns the public links on that page. It does not read the browser. The signed-in tutor also offers get_browser_reveal and get_connection_reveal .

chunks.title: Page tools for browser assistants — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: What each page offers
chunks.text: They repeat what the probe page already shows. Cookie values stay hidden. Each one returns that public view. The gotchas page also offers get_atlas_summary , lookup_atlas_technique , and lookup_gotcha . ATLAS is the Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems from MITRE. The lookup returns the public lesson. It does not include attack steps. You can give get_atlas_summary a status to keep one group. The groups are fixed, mitigated, accepted, needs-human, and not-applicable. Omit status to list every technique. not-applicable means the techniques that do not apply to this site. The lookup tools take a code or words from the name. If you give both, id wins.

chunks.title: Page tools for browser assistants — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: What each page offers
chunks.text: The result includes a short note when that happens. The architecture page also offers get_architecture_guide . It describes the four diagrams. You can pass req, auth, loop, or trust. Omit the section to get all four. It returns the title and summary of each diagram. The live demos page also offers get_demo_catalog and read_demo_state . The catalog is a fixed list. Omit the demo code to list all of them. The state tool says whether a demo is on the page and whether a result is on screen. It does not return that text. While the list is still loading, the state says so. The script injection lab counts as on the page. The widget docs pages also offer get_page_guide .

chunks.title: Page tools for browser assistants — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: What each page offers
chunks.text: It returns the headings and the links on the page you are reading. The widget home page also offers set_color , get_color , and reset_color . They change or read the example color on that page and nothing else. The swatch starts at #1f6feb. #3366ff is only a sample in the tool form. Each tool returns the color now on the swatch. The color field description is short. The allowed color names stay in the schema list. A bad color returns an error, and that error includes the allowed names.

chunks.title: Page tools for browser assistants — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: One tool definition, two callers
chunks.text: Each tool is written once. WebMCP registers that same object with document.modelContext.registerTool . The chat widget on these docs pages can use the same object when you are connected to OpenRouter. The widget reads the list and sends the tools with your question. Some fields exist so the Model Context Tool Inspector can show a sample input. Those fields are annotations , examples , and oneOf . outputSchema documents the result for tests and for future browsers. Chrome 156 does not pass outputSchema on. It is absent from getTools() . The page tools do not set default . A default made the inspector send a value even when leaving the field out would list everything.

chunks.title: Page tools for browser assistants — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: One tool definition, two callers
chunks.text: The color tool still has a sample default so a manual run can fill a color. That sample is #3366ff. It is not the starting color. The starting color is #1f6feb. The widget removes these extra fields before the call reaches OpenRouter. OpenRouter receives the tool name, the description, and a simpler input schema.

chunks.title: Page tools for browser assistants — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Why the tutor chat does not go through WebMCP
chunks.text: The tutor on the main site runs on the server. When the model asks for a tool, the server runs that tool itself. It does not ask the browser to look the tool up through WebMCP. The widget does the same kind of thing in the page. When OpenRouter asks for a tool, the widget calls the tool function directly. WebMCP is the door for an assistant this site does not own.

chunks.title: Page tools for browser assistants — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: When a server-to-page bridge makes sense
chunks.text: A bridge makes sense when the server agent needs a power that only the server has, and also needs to change or read the open page. It also makes sense as a lesson, so you can see both sides of one call. This site does not have that bridge yet. Here is how it would work. The server would define a custom tool with the same name as the page action. That name would have to be added to the allowed tools list, called ALLOWED_TOOLS in the server code. The permission handler would reject it otherwise. The tool would need a strict input schema. The page would check the input again before doing anything. The server would send the call to the open tab on the chat stream.

chunks.title: Page tools for browser assistants — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: When a server-to-page bridge makes sense
chunks.text: The page would run the action and post the result back. The server would give that result to the model. render_widget is the one-way version that already exists. The server tool emits an event. The page draws the chart. The page does not post a tool result back for the drawing itself.

chunks.title: Page tools for browser assistants — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: How the Copilot software development kit limits tools
chunks.text: The limits are already written up as gotchas. This page does not repeat them. It only points at them. The client runs in empty mode, so the built-in shell and file tools are not available. Each session offers only custom tools. In the kit that setting is availableTools set to custom:* . Read Never run the SDK in its default mode on a shared server . A permission handler runs before each tool. It denies the request unless the kind is a custom tool and the name is on the fixed list of ten. Read Every tool call goes through the permission handler: deny by default . Each tool checks its input again inside its own handler.

chunks.title: Page tools for browser assistants — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: How the Copilot software development kit limits tools
chunks.text: A name that passed the list can still be rejected if the arguments are wrong.

chunks.title: Why a client-side key is an XSS risk — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Why a client-side key is an XSS risk
chunks.text: Because the OpenRouter key lives in sessionStorage , it is readable by any JavaScript that runs on this page's origin. If an attacker could inject a script — a cross-site scripting (XSS) bug — that script could read btw_or_key and spend your OpenRouter credits. This is the honest trade-off of a backend-free, bring-your-own-key design.

chunks.title: Why a client-side key is an XSS risk — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Who bears the risk
chunks.text: The exposure is the visitor's own key and credits , not the site owner's. There is no shared server key to steal, and no other visitor is affected. Still, the site must avoid XSS, because an injected script on this origin can read the key.

chunks.title: Why a client-side key is an XSS risk — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: How the widget reduces it
